say: Every other tool in this book does something to data you hand it. This one watches the site itself. And the question it answers is not analytical, it is architectural: how do you get an event from a visitor's browser onto a dashboard, live, without polling for it?

Headline totals for whatever window is selected. Every panel on the page reads the same one response, which is why the range control is a single strip at the top rather than a setting on each of twenty panels.
Four presets and a calendar for anything else.

Event volume across the window. The green badge is the busiest hour of the trailing seven days, and it deliberately ignores the range you picked — that is a property of the site, not of the window you happen to be looking through.

Page view, then tool open, then query run, in that order. That is the drop-off worth measuring on a site like this: how many arrive, how many open something, and how many actually run it. Each step is a far stronger signal of interest than the one before.
Back to today, and there is a reason that matters in a moment. An event arriving while you are looking at last week still joins the feed, but it must not be added to statistics describing last week.
The live feed is the newest fifty events. A window, not a log. And nothing arriving is a real observation — a quiet feed means a quiet site, not a broken socket.
Now watch the top of that feed. Exporting is itself a tracked action, so this click puts a row into the very table the feed is subscribed to.

There it is. Nothing on this page polled for that. The row was committed to Postgres, the replication stream that exists so the database can recover from a crash noticed the insert, and Supabase pushed it down a WebSocket this page opened when it loaded.
That is the whole idea. Zero requests when nothing is happening, and no staleness when something is. The number changed because something happened, not because a clock ticked.
